name: Unbleached Silk
lede: Unbleached Silk is a pale, warm cream, the color of raw silk before it is washed and whitened, and the same shade the Japanese tradition calls Shironeri.

sections.title: Raw silk, two traditions
sections.body:
Our color library carries this name from two independent sources: an English color-naming source and the Japanese traditional list, where it appears as *Shironeri* (白練), literally "unbleached silk" [1]. Both point to the same fact of the craft: silk fiber comes off the cocoon pale gold-cream, not white, and only turns bright white after it is boiled and bleached [1].

Its nearest named neighbor in our library is [[alabaster]], a cooler, slightly less yellow cream (CIEDE2000 distance 2.9) [2]. Measured in LCH, Unbleached Silk sits at lightness 90, chroma 16 and hue 57 degrees, close to the pale end of the oranges family [2]. [[seashell-pink]], [[almond]] and [[desert-sand]] sit a little further off on the same warm, pale scale [2]. The ISCC-NBS system files the hue as "pale yellowish pink" (block 31) [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this cream in 57 of 23,781 paintings (0.24%, as photographed), rarer than about half the named colors we track [3]. It most often turns up as a light rather than a shadow or mid-tone, playing that role in 54% of its 39 strongest matches [3]. The earliest dated match is Filippo Lippi's work from 1441, with 42 dated paintings in all running up to 1940; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first [3]. In printed English the word pattern peaks in the 1890s, though that count mixes the color sense with silk itself as a material [3].

questions.q: Why does raw silk start out cream-colored rather than white?
choices: It has not yet been boiled and bleached
Silkworms only spin white thread when well fed
It is dyed cream before weaving
Sunlight slowly whitens it after weaving
questions.answer: It has not yet been boiled and bleached
